10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simplified contrastive loss, already covered in this topic, scoring one positive pair against several negative pairs.

code.content:
import math

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    # already covered generally as cosine similarity in Sentence Embeddings
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    norm_a = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    norm_b = math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / (norm_a * norm_b)

# already covered as data augmentation for positive pairs in this topic
anchor = [0.8, 0.3, 0.1]
positive = [0.75, 0.35, 0.15]  # a differently augmented view of the same original example

# already covered as negative pairs in this topic
negatives = [[0.1, 0.9, 0.2], [0.2, 0.1, 0.9], [0.5, 0.5, 0.1]]

def contrastive_loss(anchor, positive, negatives, temperature=0.5):
    # already covered as contrastive loss formalized in this topic
    pos_score = math.exp(cosine_similarity(anchor, positive) / temperature)
    neg_scores = sum(math.exp(cosine_similarity(anchor, neg) / temperature) for neg in negatives)
    return -math.log(pos_score / (pos_score + neg_scores))

loss = contrastive_loss(anchor, positive, negatives)
print(f"Positive pair similarity (already covered in this topic): {cosine_similarity(anchor, positive):.3f}")
for i, neg in enumerate(negatives):
    print(f"Negative pair {i} similarity: {cosine_similarity(anchor, neg):.3f}")

print(f"\nContrastive loss (already covered in this topic): {loss:.4f}")
print("A genuinely lower loss means the positive pair sits genuinely much closer than every negative pair")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Contrastive learning learns representations by pulling similar examples together, pushing others apart.
CLIP already demonstrated one concrete contrastive setup; this topic generalizes that idea.
It needs pairs of examples labeled as similar, positive, or different, negative.
Data augmentation is a common trick for creating positive pairs without any human labeling.
Training organizes the embedding space by pulling positives close and pushing negatives apart.
A contrastive loss function scores how well that pull-together, push-apart pattern is achieved.
Because positive pairs come from augmentation, no human labels are needed at all.
This makes contrastive learning a concrete, powerful instance of self-supervised learning.
